analogy.p: Imagine tiling a square floor with 1 m by 1 m tiles. If you double the width of the room, you do not need twice as many tiles but four times as many, because you need two extra rows as well as two extra columns. Now imagine filling the room with 1 m cube crates: doubling every dimension needs 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times as many crates, because the height has doubled too. The idea maps to k, k² and k³ exactly. It breaks down for real rooms with fixed-size fittings: a door or tile does not scale with the room, whereas in similar shapes every part scales by the same factor.
analogy.t: Tiling a floor and filling a box

bullets: **Linear scale factor (k):** multiplies every length (sides, heights, radii, perimeters, circumferences, diagonals, slant heights).
**Area scale factor:** k² multiplies every area (surface area, cross-section area, shaded areas, area of a face).
**Volume scale factor:** k³ multiplies every volume (and capacity).
You must be able to go **both ways**: from lengths to areas and volumes, and from areas or volumes back to lengths.
Edexcel often hides this inside a longer context question (a model, a statue, a bottle, a cone cut in half), so you have to spot that the shapes are similar.
This is **Higher tier** content; Foundation only meets simple enlargement and ratio ideas.
core.p: Edexcel Higher requires you to **use area and volume scale factors in similar shapes and solids**. You must know that if the lengths of two similar shapes are in the ratio 1 : k, then their areas are in the ratio 1 : k² and their volumes are in the ratio 1 : k³. You must be able to move in both directions between length, area and volume ratios, and to apply this to real problems such as paint, mass, capacity and cost. The topic usually appears as a 3 to 5 mark Geometry and measures question on Paper 1, 2 or 3 and is a favourite for 'grade 7 to 9' problem solving.

bullets: **Corresponding sides** are in the **same ratio**: if one side is 3 times longer, every side is 3 times longer.
**Corresponding angles are equal**: angles do not change under enlargement.
**All circles are similar**, all squares are similar, all equilateral triangles are similar, all spheres are similar and all cubes are similar.
**Not all rectangles are similar**: a 2 by 4 rectangle and a 3 by 9 rectangle have different side ratios (1 : 2 against 1 : 3).
Two cylinders are similar only if **height : radius** is the same ratio for both; two cones likewise.
You find k by dividing a length on the **new** shape by the **matching** length on the **original**: k = new length ÷ old length.
If k is bigger than 1 the shape gets larger; if k is between 0 and 1 the shape gets smaller (for example k = 1/2 halves lengths).
core.p: Two shapes are **similar** if one is an enlargement of the other, possibly rotated or reflected. In practice this means all corresponding angles are equal and all corresponding lengths are in the same ratio. The scale factor links every pair of corresponding lengths, which is why a single number k is enough to describe the enlargement. Similar is different from **congruent**: congruent shapes are identical in shape and size (k = 1), whereas similar shapes may be different sizes.

bullets: **Rectangle proof:** area = a × b. After enlargement by k the sides are ka and kb, so the new area = ka × kb = **k² × ab**.
**Cuboid proof:** volume = a × b × c. After enlargement the new volume = ka × kb × kc = **k³ × abc**.
**Square of side 1:** side 2 gives area 4 (four unit squares); side 3 gives area 9 (nine unit squares).
**Cube of side 1:** side 2 holds 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 unit cubes; side 3 holds 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 unit cubes.

The same rule holds for **curved shapes** (circles, spheres, cones, cylinders) because their formulas also contain lengths multiplied together: area of circle = πr², so doubling r multiplies area by 4.
**Perimeters and circumferences** are lengths, so they scale by k, not k².
Units tell you the dimension: cm (length), cm² (area), cm³ (volume).
core.h: Why lengths, areas and volumes scale differently
core.p: Length is one-dimensional, area is two-dimensional (length × length) and volume is three-dimensional (length × length × length). When every length is multiplied by k, an area, which is built from two lengths multiplied together, picks up the factor k twice, giving k × k = k². A volume is built from three lengths, so it picks up k three times, giving k × k × k = k³. This is the reason behind the rule, and explaining it is worth knowing for 'show that' questions.

bullets: **Length ratio** a : b gives **area ratio a² : b²** gives **volume ratio a³ : b³**.
Example: lengths 2 : 3 gives areas 4 : 9 gives volumes 8 : 27.
Example: lengths 1 : 5 gives areas 1 : 25 gives volumes 1 : 125.
Example: lengths 3 : 4 gives areas 9 : 16 gives volumes 27 : 64.
As a **scale factor from the first shape to the second**: length k, area k², volume k³.
A scale factor of **1/2** gives area factor **1/4** and volume factor **1/8**, so a half-size model has only one eighth of the volume (and, for the same material, one eighth of the mass).
Always state clearly what you are doing, for example: 'area scale factor = (3/2)² = 9/4', so that method marks are available even if you slip.
core.h: The scale factor rules and notation
core.p: Write the rules in a table so that you can use them without hesitation. If the **length ratio** is a : b, the length scale factor from the first shape to the second is k = b/a. The **area ratio** is a² : b² and the **volume ratio** is a³ : b³. Ratios can be simplified in the usual way, but you should keep the pairs in the same order (small : large, or large : small) all the way through a question so that you multiply when you should and divide when you should not.

bullets: **Step 1:** find k by dividing corresponding lengths (new ÷ old).
**Step 2:** square it to get the **area scale factor** k².
**Step 3:** multiply the original area by k² (or divide if you are going from large to small).
**Check:** a larger shape must give a larger area. If k is greater than 1 then k² is bigger than k, so areas grow more than lengths.
Example: triangles with bases 6 cm and 9 cm; small area 20 cm². k = 9/6 = 3/2; area SF = 9/4; large area = 20 × 9/4 = 45 cm².
Going back down: large area 45 cm², k = 2/3, area SF = 4/9, so 45 × 4/9 = 20 cm². Same answer both ways.
Do **not** use the length scale factor on its own for an area: that is the most common error in this topic.
core.h: Finding a missing area using area scale factor
core.p: This is the most common starting point. You are given two similar shapes, a pair of corresponding lengths and the area of one shape. Work out the **length scale factor** first, then **square it** to get the area scale factor, then multiply or divide the known area. The direction matters: multiply when going to the bigger shape and divide when going to the smaller shape. Writing 'small × SF = large' beside your working helps you avoid sign slips.

bullets: Volume SF = k³; for k = 3/2 the factor is 27/8 = 3.375.
Example: bottles 10 cm and 15 cm tall, small one holds 200 ml. k = 3/2, volume SF = 27/8 = 3.375, large bottle = 200 × 3.375 = **675 ml**.
Example: statue 20 cm tall has mass 800 g; a similar statue of the same material is 30 cm tall. Mass = 800 × (3/2)³ = 800 × 3.375 = **2700 g**.
**Mass scales with volume** only if the density is the same, which is why the question says 'same material'.
**Surface area** (paint, wrapping paper, gold plating) scales with k², not k³.
**Cross-section area** (for example of a pipe or the area of a face) scales with k².
Capacity scales as volume: 1 cm³ = 1 millilitre, 1000 cm³ = 1 litre.
core.h: Finding a missing volume or mass using volume scale factor
core.p: For solids the process is identical, except that you **cube** the length scale factor. Volume scale factor is also used for **capacity** (millilitres, litres), for **mass** when two similar objects are made of the same material (same density, mass = density × volume), and for the amount of material needed to fill an object. Surface areas, on the other hand, use the area scale factor, so a question that mentions both paint (area) and mass (volume) needs both factors.

bullets: **Area ratio to length ratio:** square root each part. 25 : 9 becomes 5 : 3.
**Volume ratio to length ratio:** cube root each part. 8 : 27 becomes 2 : 3; 64 : 125 becomes 4 : 5.
**Area ratio to volume ratio:** square root, then cube. Areas 4 : 9 give lengths 2 : 3, then volumes 8 : 27.
**Volume ratio to area ratio:** cube root, then square. Volumes 8 : 27 give lengths 2 : 3, then areas 4 : 9.
Example: areas 18 cm² and 50 cm². k² = 50/18 = 25/9, so k = 5/3, volume SF = (5/3)³ = 125/27. If the small volume is 54 cm³ the large is 54 × 125/27 = **250 cm³**.
Learn the common perfect squares and cubes: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36 and 1, 8, 27, 64, 125 so that roots are quick on a non-calculator paper.
If the numbers are **not perfect squares or cubes** use the calculator root keys and keep the full calculator value until the final answer.
core.h: Going backwards: from areas or volumes to lengths
core.p: Examiners like to give you the **area ratio** or the **volume ratio** and ask for a length. Here you need the inverse operations: take the **square root** of an area ratio to find the length ratio, and the **cube root** of a volume ratio to find the length ratio. Then, if the question wants the other measure, apply k² or k³ to the length ratio. The length ratio is always the bridge between area and volume.

bullets: Lengths increase by 10%: k = 1.1, area factor = 1.1² = 1.21, so area increases by **21%**; volume factor = 1.1³ = 1.331, so volume increases by **33.1%**.
Lengths decrease by 20%: k = 0.8, area factor = 0.64 (a **36% decrease**), volume factor = 0.512 (a **48.8% decrease**).
Lengths doubled (100% increase): area x 4 (**300% increase**), volume x 8 (**700% increase**).
Percentage change in area is **not** the same as percentage change in length: do not just copy the percentage.
Percentage change = (multiplier - 1) × 100. A multiplier of 1.21 means +21%.
The percentage change for area or volume is always **bigger in size** than the length change.
Link to compound interest: the same repeated-multiplier idea, 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1.
core.p: A common Higher twist is to give a percentage change in length and ask for the percentage change in area or volume. Convert the percentage change to a **multiplier**, which is the linear scale factor k, then square or cube it, and finally convert back to a percentage change. This is a **reverse percentage / multiplier** idea linked to compound percentages, so the working must show the multiplier clearly.

bullets: The small cone and the original cone share the same apex and the same angle, so they are **similar**; the frustum is **not** similar to either.
Use heights or radii to find k: for example heights 4 and 12 give k = 4/12 = 1/3 (small to whole).
**Small cone volume = (1/3)³ = 1/27** of the whole cone.
**Frustum volume = 1 - 1/27 = 26/27** of the whole cone.
If the whole cone has volume V, the frustum has volume **26V/27**; ratio frustum : small cone = 26 : 1.
The same trick works with pyramids: slice parallel to the base to get a smaller similar pyramid.
To find the **curved surface area** of the small cone use k², because curved surface area is an area.
core.p: A classic Higher problem cuts a cone (or pyramid) by a plane parallel to its base. The small piece cut off is a cone **similar** to the original, and what remains is a **frustum**. The frustum is not similar to anything, but you can find its volume by **subtraction**: volume of frustum = volume of whole cone - volume of small cone. The scale factor between the small cone and the whole cone is found from their heights or radii, and then the volume ratio is k³.

bullets: Always find **k** first. It is the common currency of every question.
If the question gives **two areas**, divide to find the area scale factor, then square-root to find k.
If the question gives **two volumes**, divide to find the volume scale factor, then cube-root to find k.
If it gives **a length of one shape and an area of the other**, use the length in a ratio with the matching length to get k.
Check that your **units** match the quantity requested (cm, cm², cm³).
Check the **size sense**: a model that is smaller than the real object must have smaller area and volume than the object.
Present answers to a suitable degree of accuracy (3 significant figures unless told otherwise).
core.p: Harder questions give you one piece of information about areas and ask for volumes, or the other way round, usually using two different units or contexts (for example surface area of a model against the volume of a real object). Do not try to jump straight from area to volume: always pass through the **length scale factor**. Write each step on its own line: SF for area, then k, then SF for volume, then the final calculation. This also earns method marks even if the final answer is wrong.

bullets: **Paint, wrapping paper, label, tiles, grass seed:** area, use k².
**Water, sand, concrete, capacity, filling:** volume, use k³.
**Mass or weight** of objects made of the same material: volume, use k³.
**Model of a building, ship or statue:** lengths are ratio of model to real object; areas and volumes need squaring and cubing.
**Cost proportional to area (for example price of a pizza by area):** use k².
**Similar triangles in a diagram** (parallel lines): the same linear scale factor works, and then areas use k².
**Maps:** a 1 : 25000 map scale is a length ratio; real area = map area × 25000² (watch the units, convert cm² to km²).
core.h: Common contexts and how to spot them
core.p: Edexcel wraps the same idea in many everyday stories. Whenever you see the words 'similar', 'mathematically similar', 'scale model', 'enlargement' or two objects with the same shape but different sizes, you should think about scale factors. Then ask yourself what the question is measuring: a length (k), a region (k²) or an amount of space or mass (k³).

bullets: **Enlargement:** a scale factor of k always multiplies lengths by k, areas by k², and leaves angles unchanged.
**Similar triangles:** find the length scale factor from parallel lines, then use it for areas.
**Area and volume formulas:** surface area of a sphere 4πr² has k²; volume 4/3 πr³ has k³.
**Density = mass ÷ volume:** same density means mass scales as volume.
**Compound measures and percentages:** repeated multiplier ideas appear when lengths change by a percentage.
**Algebra:** you may be asked to show that area scale factor is k², using sides ka and kb.
**Direct proportion:** area is proportional to length squared, volume to length cubed (y proportional to x²), which links to proportionality statements in algebra.
core.p: This topic ties together several parts of the GCSE course, so revision of it also supports other questions. It builds on **ratio and proportion**, **enlargement** and **similar triangles**, and on area and volume formulas for circles, cylinders, cones and spheres. At Higher tier it can also combine with algebra (using k as a variable), with rearranging formulae, and with **density, mass and volume** in problem solving.

bullets: If the ratio of areas is **a : b** then the ratio of lengths is **√a : √b**; with non-square numbers leave answers as surds or use a calculator.
If told that the volume of one solid is **n times** the other, then the length scale factor is the cube root of n.
If the **difference** of two volumes is given, set up volume small = V and large = V × k³, so the difference is V(k³ - 1).
Use algebra: if the length scale factor is x, areas are in the ratio 1 : x² and volumes 1 : x³.
For 'show that' questions, write the scale factors clearly, show the substitution, and state the conclusion.
Hollow or thick-walled objects: the **thickness** also scales by k, so a scaled model of a hollow object is not just the same wall thickness.
Be ready to rearrange: small volume = large volume ÷ k³.
core.p: At grades 8 and 9 you may meet multi-step problems that need algebra or reasoning. Typical examples include a cone cut into a frustum, two similar solids with a given **difference** in volume, an area ratio that must be turned into a volume ratio for a combined shape, or a request to 'prove' a result. Treat these as normal scale-factor problems with extra algebra, and keep your working structured so the examiner can follow your reasoning.

bullets: Write **'length SF = ...'**, **'area SF = ...'** or **'volume SF = ...'** explicitly.
Label units carefully: cm² for area, cm³ for volume.
A **calculator is not allowed on Paper 1** so know the squares up to 15² and cubes up to 5³ or 10³.
Reasonableness check: if you scale up, the answer must be bigger; if you scale down, smaller.
Do not round intermediate steps; round only the final answer.
Underline the **given measure** (area, volume or length) and the **required measure**.
If stuck, assume **k = a simple number** like 2 and test your method on a unit square or cube to check which power applies.
core.p: Scale factor questions are short on calculation but long on reasoning. Marks are mostly for stating the correct scale factor and then using it in the correct direction. Show each step: the length scale factor, the area or volume scale factor, then the final answer with units. Because the topic is often placed near the end of a paper, it is easy to rush; slow down and decide whether you are in 1D, 2D or 3D before you calculate.

exam: **Command words:** 'work out', 'calculate', 'find' need a numerical answer with units; 'show that' needs every step written with a final statement; 'explain' needs a sentence.
**Typical marks:** 2 to 3 marks for a one-step scale factor question (M1 for the correct scale factor or ratio, A1 for the answer); 4 to 5 marks for multi-step problems.
**Method mark (M1)** is usually for the correct **scale factor** (for example (3/2)² or 125/27), so always write it down even if you go wrong later.
Model phrase: **'area scale factor = (length scale factor)²'** and 'volume scale factor = (length scale factor)³'.
For a **'show that' 3 mark question**, write: find length SF, convert to area/volume SF, substitute, conclude with the required value.
In a **6 mark problem** (for example a bottle, a model and paint), set out the plan: find k, then area SF, then volume SF, then answer each part with units.
If given areas or volumes, **state the root** you take: 'length ratio = √(area ratio)' or '∛(volume ratio)'.
Always write the **ratio order** (small : large) and keep it consistent through the whole question.
Know squares up to 15² and cubes 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000 for non-calculator papers.
Check the **answer is reasonable** (bigger shape gives bigger area and volume) and the units are right.
Quote **a sensible degree of accuracy**: 3 significant figures if not exact, or leave as an exact fraction/ratio when the question asks for a ratio.

mistakes.r: Square k for area (k²) and cube k for volume (k³): doubling lengths gives 4 times the area and 8 times the volume.
mistakes.w: Using the length scale factor for areas or volumes (for example doubling lengths so area is doubled).

mistakes.r: Decide first whether the quantity is a length, an area or a volume: 1D uses k, 2D uses k², 3D uses k³.
mistakes.w: Squaring when you should cube, or the other way round, e.g. using k² for a volume question.

mistakes.r: Check the direction: to go to a smaller shape use a scale factor less than 1 (or divide); the answer must be smaller.
mistakes.w: Multiplying by the scale factor when going from the larger shape to the smaller (should divide or use 1/k).

mistakes.r: Square root an area ratio to get the length ratio (4 : 9 gives 2 : 3) and cube root a volume ratio.
mistakes.w: Taking the ratio of areas as the ratio of lengths (e.g. areas 4 : 9 so lengths 4 : 9).

mistakes.r: Use cm² for area and cm³ for volume, and state the units in the final answer.
mistakes.w: Writing area units as cm or volume units as cm² or cm.

mistakes.r: Check that corresponding sides are in the same ratio; only then are the shapes similar and the rule applies.
mistakes.w: Assuming every pair of shapes with the same name is similar (e.g. any two rectangles or cylinders).

mistakes.r: Convert to a multiplier: 1.1² = 1.21, so area increases by 21% (and volume by 33.1%).
mistakes.w: Saying a 10% increase in length gives a 10% increase in area.

mistakes.r: Paint, surface area and cross-section use k²; mass (same material), capacity and volume use k³.
mistakes.w: Using area scale factor for mass, or volume scale factor for paint.

mistakes.r: Frustum volume = whole cone - small cone; the small cone has volume k³ × whole.
mistakes.w: Forgetting that the frustum is not similar to the original cone and subtracting nothing.

mistakes.r: Keep k exact (a fraction) or full calculator value and round only the final answer.
mistakes.w: Rounding too early, e.g. rounding k to 1.7 then cubing.

summary: Edexcel Higher asks you to use scale factors in similar shapes and solids: if lengths are in the ratio 1 : k then areas are in the ratio 1 : k² and volumes in the ratio 1 : k³, and you must work in both directions between them and apply them to paint, mass, capacity, percentage change and sliced cones. It matters because it appears as a multi-mark problem-solving question on every Higher paper.

terms.d: Shapes where all corresponding angles are equal and all corresponding sides are in the same ratio (one is an enlargement of the other).
Shapes that are identical in shape and size; one can be moved onto the other by rotation, reflection or translation.
The number by which every length in a shape is multiplied to produce a similar shape; written k.
The number by which every area is multiplied in similar shapes; equal to k² where k is the linear scale factor.
The number by which every volume is multiplied in similar solids; equal to k³.
Sides that occupy the same position in two similar shapes and are related by the scale factor.
A transformation that changes the size of a shape by a scale factor from a centre while keeping its shape.
A comparison of quantities written a : b; for similar shapes the ratio of lengths is a : b, areas a² : b² and volumes a³ : b³.
The solid that remains when a smaller cone or pyramid is cut off the top by a plane parallel to its base.
The volume of liquid or gas a container can hold, measured in ml or litres (1 ml = 1 cm³).
Mass per unit volume: density = mass ÷ volume; same material means same density.
The total area of all the faces of a solid; scales by k² in similar solids.
The shape you get when you cut through a solid; its area scales by k² in similar solids.
The number you multiply by to apply a percentage change, for example 1.1 for a 10% increase; equals k for lengths.
The exam wording meaning that all lengths are in proportion and angles are equal, so scale factors can be used.
Inverse operations used to turn an area ratio or volume ratio back into a length ratio.

worked.q: Triangle A and triangle B are similar. The base of A is 6 cm and the base of B is 9 cm. The area of A is 20 cm². Work out the area of B. [3 marks]
steps: Length scale factor from A to B: k = 9 ÷ 6 = 3/2. [M1]
Check: B is bigger so its area is bigger; 45 is greater than 20, so the answer is sensible.

worked.q: Two similar cones have volumes 24 cm³ and 81 cm³. The smaller cone has height 8 cm and curved surface area 40 cm². Work out (a) the height of the larger cone and (b) the curved surface area of the larger cone. [5 marks]
steps: Length scale factor k = cube root of 27/8 = 3/2. [M1]

worked.q: Two similar solids have surface areas 18 cm² and 50 cm². The volume of the smaller solid is 54 cm³. Work out the volume of the larger solid. [4 marks]
steps: Check: lengths up by 5/3 so volume up by about 4.6, and 54 × 4.6 is about 250.
